title: Parables of the Kingdom
summary: Teaching from a boat, Jesus tells the parable of the sower and explains to his disciples why he speaks in parables. He adds parables of weeds among wheat, a mustard seed, leaven, hidden treasure, a pearl, and a dragnet, and explains two of them. Returning to Nazareth, he is rejected by his own town, and he does few miracles there because of their unbelief.
story: Chapters 11 and 12 showed Jesus meeting doubt, indifference, and hostility, and dividing people into those who oppose him and those who do the Father's will. Chapter 13 explains that division. If the kingdom of heaven has arrived, why do so many refuse it, and why does it look so small? The parables answer: the message is like seed that falls on different kinds of soil; the kingdom begins small and grows; good and evil will grow side by side until the end; and those who see its worth give up everything for it. This is the third of Matthew's five great discourses, standing at the center of the Gospel. The chapter ends with the rejection at Nazareth, a living example of the hard soil the parables describe.
historical:
The phrase kingdom of heaven, which appears in almost every parable here, is Matthew's usual way of saying what Mark and Luke call the kingdom of God. Many Jews of the time avoided saying God's name out of reverence, and heaven was a common respectful substitute, so the two phrases mean the same thing: God's reign, not a place in the sky. Jewish hopes in the Second Temple period generally expected God's kingdom to arrive all at once, with the defeat of Israel's enemies and the judgment of the wicked. The parables of this chapter describe something different: a kingdom already present in Jesus' ministry but hidden, small, and resisted, whose full arrival and final judgment still lie ahead.

The parables of the sower and the mustard seed have parallels in Mark 4 and in Luke 8 and 13, and the leaven appears also in Luke 13. The rejection at Nazareth is also told in Mark 6, and Luke 4:16-30 gives a fuller account set at the start of the ministry. The weeds, the treasure, the pearl, and the net are found only in Matthew. Nazareth was a small village in the hills of lower Galilee, a few miles from the larger town of Sepphoris, which Herod Antipas rebuilt as his capital in the years of Jesus' youth.
cultural:
Every image comes from ordinary Galilean life. Farmers scattered seed by hand, and seed fell on paths packed hard by foot traffic, on thin soil over limestone, and among thorn roots. A yield of thirty, sixty, or a hundredfold would have sounded extraordinary. The weed in verse 25 is most often identified with darnel, a grass that looks very like wheat until it heads and whose seeds are harmful to eat. The mustard plant grows from a tiny seed into a shrub several feet high, and the smallness of the mustard seed was proverbial. Leaven was a lump of fermented dough kept back from the last batch; elsewhere in Scripture it often stands for corruption, but here it pictures hidden, pervasive growth. Three measures of flour is a very large batch, enough to feed a crowd.

In a land often crossed by armies, people buried valuables for safekeeping, and hoards were sometimes lost when the owner died. Pearls were among the most prized luxuries of the Roman world. The dragnet was a large net drawn between boats or hauled to shore, catching everything in its path; fish without fins and scales were unclean under Leviticus 11 and would be thrown out. At Nazareth, the townspeople know Jesus' family: his father was a tekton, a builder or craftsman in wood or stone, and they name his brothers and mention his sisters. Who these brothers and sisters were is debated among Christians. Many Protestants take them as children of Mary and Joseph born after Jesus; the Orthodox tradition has generally held that they were children of Joseph from an earlier marriage; the Catholic tradition, following Jerome, has generally taken them as close relatives such as cousins, holding to Mary's perpetual virginity.
literary: A parable (parabole) is a comparison drawn from life that invites the hearer to see something familiar in a new light. The Hebrew counterpart, mashal, could mean a proverb, a riddle, or an extended story. The chapter is built with care. The first half is spoken to the crowds by the sea (verses 1 to 35), and the second half to the disciples in the house (verses 36 to 52). The sower and the weeds each receive an explanation, while the short parables come in pairs: mustard seed and leaven (small beginnings, great outcome), treasure and pearl (joyful sacrifice for supreme value). The weeds and the net both end at the close of the age with separation. The saying about the scribe of the kingdom (verse 52), who brings out treasures new and old, may be Matthew's description of his own work. Since the late nineteenth century scholars have debated whether parables should be read as having one main point, as Adolf Julicher argued, or whether they can contain several points of comparison; the explanations Jesus gives in this chapter show that some parables at least carry allegorical detail, while the short parables make a single point.

outline.t: The mustard seed and the leaven
The hidden treasure and the pearl
The dragnet; scribes of the kingdom

doctrines.note: The chapter teaches that God's kingdom is already present in Jesus but hidden and growing, mixed with evil in the world until the end of the age, when it will be revealed and the wicked separated from the righteous. Theologians often describe this as already and not yet: begun in Jesus' ministry, completed at his return.

The mysteries of the kingdom are given to the disciples, not discovered by them. Parables reveal to those who come to Jesus for understanding and conceal from those who do not, so that the same story becomes light or judgment depending on the hearer.

The weeds and the net both end in separation at the end of the age, carried out by angels at the Son of Man's command. The servants are forbidden to uproot the weeds themselves: final judgment belongs to God, not to his people.

The sower shows that hearing is not enough: the word must be understood, rooted, and allowed to bear fruit despite trouble, worry, and wealth. At Nazareth unbelief limits what Jesus does, not because his power fails but because they will not receive him.

words.note: Parabole, parable, literally something set beside another for comparison. It covers short sayings, similes, and full stories. Matthew uses it twelve times in this chapter, which is the heart of his teaching on how the kingdom works.

Musterion, mystery or secret. In Jewish writings of the period, including Daniel 2 in the Greek Old Testament, it means a secret of God's plan that he reveals to those he chooses. It is not a puzzle to be solved by cleverness but a truth that must be disclosed. The mystery here is that the kingdom has come in Jesus in an unexpected, hidden form.

Zizanion, weeds, most likely darnel, which resembles wheat in its early growth. The resemblance is the point: in the present age the children of the kingdom and the children of the evil one cannot always be told apart, and an attempt to root one out would harm the other.

Sunteleia, completion or consummation. With aion (age) it forms the phrase the end of the age (verses 39, 40, 49), which Matthew alone among the Gospels uses, and which returns in 24:3 and in Jesus' final promise in 28:20. It marks history as moving toward a goal set by God.

christ: Jesus is the sower in the explanation of the weeds: the Son of Man sows the good seed, owns the field, and will send his angels at the end. The kingdom is his kingdom (verse 41). The parables also reveal him by their very form. Matthew quotes Psalm 78:2 (“I will open My mouth in parables”), where the psalmist retells Israel's history as a lesson, and applies it to Jesus, who utters things hidden since the foundation of the world. The disciples are told that prophets and righteous people longed to see what they see: the promises of the Old Testament are being fulfilled in front of them. The treasure and the pearl are often read as Christ himself or the kingdom he brings, worth more than everything a person owns, though the parables speak of the kingdom rather than naming him. At Nazareth, the one who teaches the mysteries of heaven is dismissed as the carpenter's son, a first taste of the rejection that will end at the cross.

hard.q: Does Jesus tell parables in order to keep people from understanding and being saved?
hard.a: Verses 10 to 15 seem to say that Jesus speaks in parables so that some will not understand, quoting Isaiah 6:9-10, where God sends Isaiah to a people whose hearts have grown dull. Readers have answered in several ways. Matthew's wording emphasizes cause: Jesus speaks in parables because (not in order that, as Mark 4:12 can be read) they see without seeing. On this reading, parables do not create hardness but expose and confirm a hardness already present, while inviting those willing to ask for more; the disciples, after all, understand only because they come and ask. Others emphasize God's sovereignty in judgment, as in Isaiah: persistent rejection of God's word brings the judgment of further blindness, and the parables are part of that judgment on a generation that has rejected John and Jesus (chapters 11 and 12). Many interpreters hold both together: God's judgment and human responsibility meet in the same act. Verse 12 states the principle that those who receive light receive more, while those who refuse it lose even what they had. The passage does not teach that anyone who wants to understand is shut out; the invitation “He who has ears, let him hear” recurs through the chapter (verses 9 and 43).

questions: Which of the four soils best describes your hearing of God's word right now, and what are the thorns or rocks in your case?
The servants wanted to pull up the weeds, and the master said wait. Where are you tempted to judge who is wheat and who is weeds?
The man with the treasure sold everything in his joy. What would it look like for your devotion to Jesus to be marked by that kind of joy rather than grim sacrifice?
